text: Last lesson's scalar function returned one value and paid a real performance price for it. This lesson's function returns a whole table instead — and because of how it's written, the optimizer never has to treat it as a black box.

Create function dbo dot ProductsBySubcategory, taking a subcategory ID, returns table, as return, a single SELECT in parentheses. That's the entire body — no BEGIN/END, no separate variable table. Just one query, with a parameter plugged into its WHERE clause.

You call it in FROM, not SELECT, because it hands back rows. SELECT star from dbo dot ProductsBySubcategory of 1 works exactly like querying a table. And because it IS a table in every way that matters, you can join it to SalesOrderDetail and SalesOrderHeader just like you would any other table.

Here's why that avoids last lesson's trap. Because the entire body is one SELECT, SQL Server can substitute that SELECT directly into the calling query, expand the parameter, and optimize the whole thing as a single combined plan. There's no separate row-by-row execution to call, because there's no separate execution at all — the optimizer sees straight through it, the same way it already treats a parameterized view.

That's the mental model to keep: a view is a saved SELECT you query like a table. An inline table-valued function is the same idea with a parameter slot. Anywhere you've reached for a view but wished you could filter it with an argument instead of bolting on a WHERE clause afterward, this is the tool.
Next lesson looks at the other kind of table-valued function — one that trades away this inlining in exchange for a BEGIN/END body that can run multiple statements.
